unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A government exists mainly to protect life and liberty. Which ideal explains the rights being protected?
choices: Natural rights
Limited government
Republicanism
Popular sovereignty
unit1-concept-practice.why: NATURAL RIGHTS belong to people before government exists. Life and liberty are the clearest clues.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: People authorize a government, and the government promises to protect their rights. Which concept describes the whole agreement?
choices: Consent of the governed
Social contract
Equality
Republicanism
unit1-concept-practice.why: The SOCIAL CONTRACT is the full exchange: authority from the people for protection of their rights.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A constitution begins by announcing that its authority comes from the people. Which ideal is most direct?
choices: Popular sovereignty
Limited government
Natural rights
Elite democracy
unit1-concept-practice.why: POPULAR SOVEREIGNTY answers where government power originates: with the people.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: The law places firm restrictions on what public officials may do. Which ideal is most direct?
choices: Equality
Republicanism
Limited government
Social contract
unit1-concept-practice.why: LIMITED GOVERNMENT means public power is restricted rather than absolute.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Voters choose the officials who will exercise government power. Which ideal focuses on that authorization?
choices: Consent of the governed
Popular sovereignty
Natural rights
Equality
unit1-concept-practice.why: CONSENT OF THE GOVERNED is demonstrated when people authorize officials through elections.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Citizens elect lawmakers to make policy instead of voting on every national law themselves. Which principle?
choices: Direct democracy
Republicanism
Social contract
Limited government
unit1-concept-practice.why: REPUBLICANISM means people govern through elected representatives.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A movement demands that a group excluded from voting receive the same political rights as other citizens. Which ideal?
choices: Equality
Elite democracy
Federalism
Pluralism
unit1-concept-practice.why: EQUALITY includes equal political rights and extending democratic participation to people who were excluded.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which description best fits a representative republic?
choices: Citizens vote personally on every law.
A monarch selects government leaders.
Voters choose officials to govern for them.
Experts govern without public elections.
unit1-concept-practice.why: A REPRESENTATIVE REPUBLIC uses elected officials to make public decisions on behalf of citizens.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Voters choose officials to govern for them.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which feature is expected in a liberal democracy?
choices: Guaranteed income equality
Competitive elections and protected rights
Rule by one permanent political party
Unlimited power for elected majorities
unit1-concept-practice.why: A LIBERAL DEMOCRACY combines competitive elections with civil liberties, minority rights, political equality, and a free press.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: The Declaration lists abuses committed without the people’s approval. Which idea do those complaints most directly challenge?
choices: Consent of the governed
Elite democracy
Judicial review
Federalism
unit1-concept-practice.why: Government actions imposed without public authorization violate CONSENT OF THE GOVERNED.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: The Constitution grants powers but divides them among branches that can check one another. Which ideal does that design protect?
choices: Natural rights
Limited government
Participatory democracy
Equality
unit1-concept-practice.why: Divided power and checks make it harder for any official or institution to exercise unlimited authority.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which sequence best captures the logic behind the founding ideals?
choices: Rights → government → consent → limits → representation
Government → elites → rights → factions → voting
Representation → monarchy → consent → unlimited power
Equality → courts → groups → government → rights
unit1-concept-practice.why: People possess RIGHTS, create GOVERNMENT, give CONSENT, place LIMITS on power, and use REPRESENTATION.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Voters approve or reject a proposed state law themselves through a referendum. Which model is most direct?
choices: Elite democracy
Pluralist democracy
Participatory democracy
Representative republic
unit1-concept-practice.why: A REFERENDUM is a strong clue for PARTICIPATORY DEMOCRACY because citizens decide policy directly.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A city invites thousands of residents to speak, organize, and help shape a new public-safety plan. Which model?
choices: Participatory democracy
Elite democracy
Pluralist democracy
Limited government
unit1-concept-practice.why: PARTICIPATORY DEMOCRACY emphasizes broad citizen involvement in political decisions.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Business, labor, environmental, and consumer organizations compete to influence the same bill. Which model?
choices: Participatory democracy
Elite democracy
Pluralist democracy
Direct democracy
unit1-concept-practice.why: PLURALIST DEMOCRACY features organized groups competing to influence public policy.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A policy emerges from bargaining and compromise among several organized interests. Which model best explains the result?
choices: Elite democracy
Pluralist democracy
Participatory democracy
Popular sovereignty
unit1-concept-practice.why: PLURALISM expects competing groups to bargain, form coalitions, and produce compromise.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A small number of wealthy, connected people have much more access to policymakers than ordinary citizens. Which model describes this concentration?
choices: Participatory democracy
Elite democracy
Pluralist democracy
Direct democracy
unit1-concept-practice.why: ELITE DEMOCRACY emphasizes the disproportionate influence of people with wealth, status, expertise, or connections.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Elected officials and specialists study technical evidence and make the final policy choice. Which model is most direct?
choices: Elite democracy
Participatory democracy
Pluralist democracy
Consent of the governed
unit1-concept-practice.why: ELITE DEMOCRACY gives leaders and experts the strongest role in making policy.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A critic says group competition has an “upper-class accent” because many people lack money or organization. What is being criticized?
choices: Participatory democracy
Pluralist democracy
Popular sovereignty
Republicanism
unit1-concept-practice.why: This is a criticism of PLURALISM: group competition may exist, but access and resources are not distributed equally.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: What is the main difference between pluralist and elite theories?
choices: Pluralism stresses many competing groups; elite theory stresses concentrated influence.
Pluralism rejects elections; elite theory requires referendums.
Pluralism protects rights; elite theory creates natural rights.
Pluralism uses experts; elite theory uses only voters.
unit1-concept-practice.why: PLURALISM distributes influence among many competing groups; ELITE THEORY sees influence concentrated among relatively few people.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Pluralism stresses many competing groups; elite theory stresses concentrated influence.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which comparison of participatory and pluralist democracy is accurate?
choices: Participation centers on citizens; pluralism centers on organized groups.
Participation centers on experts; pluralism centers on judges.
Participation limits voting; pluralism eliminates lobbying.
Participation requires a republic; pluralism requires monarchy.
unit1-concept-practice.why: PARTICIPATORY DEMOCRACY emphasizes citizen involvement. PLURALIST DEMOCRACY emphasizes competition among organized groups.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Participation centers on citizens; pluralism centers on organized groups.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which clue points most clearly to elite democracy rather than pluralist democracy?
choices: Many organizations present competing plans.
Several coalitions negotiate a compromise.
A small network dominates access and decisions.
Interest groups lobby members of Congress.
unit1-concept-practice.why: Concentrated access and decision-making are ELITE clues. Competition among many groups is the pluralist clue.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: A small network dominates access and decisions.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: What is Brutus No. 1’s central worry about a very large republic?
choices: Citizens will vote too frequently.
Representatives may not know or express local views.
States will control too much foreign policy.
Factions will disappear completely.
unit1-concept-practice.why: BRUTUS worries that a large republic creates distant representation that cannot accurately express the people’s views.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Representatives may not know or express local views.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Why does Brutus care about the number and character of representatives?
choices: They must accurately express the people’s views.
They must remain wealthy enough to avoid voting.
They must eliminate every organized interest.
They must serve without facing elections.
unit1-concept-practice.why: For Brutus, people do not truly govern if their representatives do not know and speak their sentiments.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: They must accurately express the people’s views.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Brutus’s warning most directly highlights tension between which two models?
choices: Pluralist and direct democracy
Participatory and elite democracy
Federal and unitary government
Natural rights and equality
unit1-concept-practice.why: Brutus fears rule drifting toward a small, distant set of representatives instead of meaningful participation by the people.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: In Federalist No. 10, what is a faction?
choices: A branch checking another branch
A group united by a shared interest
A court rejecting a precedent
A state refusing a national law
unit1-concept-practice.why: In FEDERALIST NO. 10, a FACTION is a group united by a shared interest that may work against others’ rights or the public good.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: A group united by a shared interest

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Why does Madison prefer a large republic for controlling factions?
choices: It removes disagreement among citizens.
It creates many interests that compete.
It allows citizens to vote on every law.
It gives one group permanent control.
unit1-concept-practice.why: A larger political sphere contains more interests, making it harder for one faction to form a lasting majority and dominate.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: It creates many interests that compete.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Why does Federalist No. 10 favor representation over pure democracy?
choices: Representatives may refine public views toward the common good.
Representatives guarantee that factions disappear.
Representatives prevent citizens from voting in elections.
Representatives return power to a monarch.
unit1-concept-practice.why: Madison argues that elected representatives can REFINE public views, though he admits corrupt representatives remain a risk.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Representatives may refine public views toward the common good.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which constitutional feature most directly reflects Madison’s representative solution?
choices: Voters choose House members at regular elections.
Judges receive compensation while serving.
States may conduct property inspections.
Presidents must meet an age requirement.
unit1-concept-practice.why: Regular election of House members connects public views to a representative institution.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Voters choose House members at regular elections.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: How does the Constitution filter public preferences?
choices: It requires every law to pass a national referendum.
It divides decisions among elected offices and institutions.
It prevents organized groups from contacting Congress.
It gives all policy decisions to state voters.
unit1-concept-practice.why: The Constitution uses REPRESENTATION and INSTITUTIONAL FILTERS: public wishes pass through elected officials, branches, and procedures.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: It divides decisions among elected offices and institutions.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement correctly separates popular sovereignty from consent of the governed?
choices: Sovereignty is the source; consent is authorization.
Sovereignty limits power; consent creates rights.
Sovereignty means courts; consent means federalism.
Sovereignty protects speech; consent divides branches.
unit1-concept-practice.why: POPULAR SOVEREIGNTY identifies the people as the source of power. CONSENT explains how people authorize government.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Sovereignty is the source; consent is authorization.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement correctly separates natural rights from limited government?
choices: Rights belong to people; limits restrict government.
Rights choose officials; limits create elections.
Rights divide branches; limits create equality.
Rights come from law; limits come from factions.
unit1-concept-practice.why: NATURAL RIGHTS belong to people. LIMITED GOVERNMENT restricts public power so those rights are not violated.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Rights belong to people; limits restrict government.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement correctly separates social contract from consent of the governed?
choices: The contract is the full agreement; consent is authorization.
The contract means elections; consent means courts.
The contract divides power; consent protects property.
The contract creates factions; consent creates experts.
unit1-concept-practice.why: The SOCIAL CONTRACT is the larger exchange of authority for protection. CONSENT focuses on the people’s authorization.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: The contract is the full agreement; consent is authorization.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement correctly separates direct from representative democracy?
choices: Direct uses citizen policy votes; representative uses elected lawmakers.
Direct uses courts; representative uses interest groups.
Direct protects rights; representative limits government.
Direct uses experts; representative uses monarchs.
unit1-concept-practice.why: In DIRECT DEMOCRACY citizens decide policy themselves. In REPRESENTATIVE DEMOCRACY elected officials decide for them.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Direct uses citizen policy votes; representative uses elected lawmakers.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: The Constitution forbids Congress from using several named powers. Which ideal is most direct?
choices: Natural rights
Popular sovereignty
Social contract
Limited government
unit1-concept-practice.why: A list of powers government may not use is direct evidence of LIMITED GOVERNMENT.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: House members are chosen by voters in regular elections. Which ideal is most directly demonstrated?
choices: Consent of the governed
Elite democracy
Federalism
Natural rights
unit1-concept-practice.why: Elections allow citizens to authorize representatives, demonstrating CONSENT OF THE GOVERNED.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A president can be investigated and removed for abusing office. Which ideal does this demonstrate?
choices: Popular sovereignty
Limited government
Pluralism
Direct democracy
unit1-concept-practice.why: Even the president is subject to constitutional rules and consequences under LIMITED GOVERNMENT.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: A movement argues that people denied the vote cannot truly approve laws imposed on them. Which ideal is being applied?
choices: Consent of the governed
Elite democracy
Judicial review
Federalism
unit1-concept-practice.why: Without political participation, the excluded group cannot give meaningful CONSENT to government authority.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: An argument says government should rarely direct how private people use their property or businesses. Which ideal is most relevant?
choices: Popular sovereignty
Limited government
Pluralist democracy
Republicanism
unit1-concept-practice.why: The argument calls for restricting government interference, which most directly supports LIMITED GOVERNMENT.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which comparison correctly matches the policy process to the democratic model?
choices: Referendum—participatory; group lobbying—pluralist
Referendum—elite; group lobbying—participatory
Expert panel—pluralist; public vote—elite
Group competition—direct; elections—pluralist
unit1-concept-practice.why: Direct citizen decisions are PARTICIPATORY; competition among organized groups is PLURALIST.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claim that participatory democracy keeps government responsive to ordinary people?
choices: Brutus warns distant representatives may not know local views.
Federalist No. 10 praises a larger political sphere.
The Constitution gives senators six-year terms.
Pluralism allows organizations to form coalitions.
unit1-concept-practice.why: Brutus supplies evidence that distance can weaken representation, supporting a claim for stronger public participation.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Brutus warns distant representatives may not know local views.

unit1-concept-practice.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claim that pluralist democracy can limit domination by one interest?
choices: Brutus says a large republic cannot represent local views.
Federalist No. 10 says many interests make one-faction control harder.
The Constitution gives judges life tenure.
Elite theory emphasizes unequal political resources.
unit1-concept-practice.why: Federalist No. 10 supports the reasoning that a large, diverse sphere makes lasting control by one faction more difficult.
unit1-concept-practice.correct: Federalist No. 10 says many interests make one-faction control harder.

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: After independence, why did the states first create a weak national government?
choices: They feared replacing one powerful ruler with another
They wanted Congress to control every state law
They wanted a president with broad emergency powers
They believed courts should collect national taxes
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The Revolution was fought against concentrated power. The Articles protected STATE SOVEREIGNTY by keeping most power in the states.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: They feared replacing one powerful ruler with another

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which choice best describes the main problem the framers were trying to solve in 1787?
choices: Give government enough power to act while still limiting it
Let state governments conduct foreign policy alone
Replace elected representatives with direct democracy
Make constitutional change possible by a simple majority
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The Constitution tried to balance effective national power with LIMITED GOVERNMENT and protection against tyranny.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Give government enough power to act while still limiting it

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: A constitution gives Congress new powers but divides national power among three branches. What does that combination show?
choices: Power can be strengthened and still restrained
Only state governments can protect liberty
Majority rule should have no limits
National laws should be optional for states
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The national government became stronger, but SEPARATION OF POWERS and CHECKS AND BALANCES limited how that power could be used.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Power can be strengthened and still restrained

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Why did many Anti-Federalists demand a bill of rights?
choices: They feared the new national government could threaten individual liberty
They wanted Congress to choose state governors
They wanted to eliminate state governments
They wanted the president to write amendments
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Anti-Federalists worried that a stronger national government might abuse its power, so they demanded written protections for individual rights.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: They feared the new national government could threaten individual liberty

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: A critic says the national government is too distant to understand local needs. Which writer’s argument does this resemble?
choices: Brutus No. 1
Federalist No. 10
The Preamble
The Gettysburg Address
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: BRUTUS NO. 1 argues that a large republic would make representatives distant from the people and threaten state power and liberty.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Brutus No. 1

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Madison argues that a large republic can control the effects of factions. What is his reasoning?
choices: Many competing interests make domination by one faction harder
A large republic prevents groups from forming
National leaders can outlaw unpopular opinions
Citizens will agree on nearly every issue
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: FEDERALIST NO. 10 says factions are unavoidable. A large republic contains many interests that compete and check one another.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Many competing interests make domination by one faction harder

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement best compares Federalist No. 10 and Brutus No. 1?
choices: Madison trusts a large republic; Brutus fears distant national power
Madison favors direct democracy; Brutus favors monarchy
Madison wants weaker representation; Brutus wants no states
Madison rejects factions; Brutus says factions never form
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Madison believes representation across a large republic can control factions. Brutus believes that same size and power will weaken genuine representation.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Madison trusts a large republic; Brutus fears distant national power

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which constitutional feature would most concern Brutus?
choices: The Supremacy Clause placing valid federal law above state law
Two-year terms for House members
The protection of jury trials
The reservation of undelegated powers to states
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Brutus feared that broad national power would overwhelm the states. The SUPREMACY CLAUSE would sharpen that concern.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: The Supremacy Clause placing valid federal law above state law

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Congress asks the states for money, but several states refuse. Which weakness of the Articles does this reveal?
choices: Congress could not tax individuals directly
Congress could remove state governors
Congress controlled too much interstate trade
Congress had an overly powerful executive
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Under the Articles, Congress could request money but lacked an effective independent power to raise revenue through taxes.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Congress could not tax individuals directly

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Two states place tariffs on each other’s goods and Congress cannot settle the dispute. What power is missing?
choices: The power to regulate interstate commerce
The power to appoint local mayors
The power to set voting ages
The power to approve state constitutions
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Congress could not effectively regulate INTERSTATE COMMERCE, allowing states to create conflicting trade rules.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: The power to regulate interstate commerce

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: An armed uprising threatens public order, but the national government cannot respond effectively. What did this suggest after Shays’ Rebellion?
choices: The country needed stronger national capacity to maintain order
The states needed separate foreign policies
Congress needed fewer ways to raise revenue
The national government already had too much military power
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: SHAYS’ REBELLION became evidence that the Articles left the national government too weak to address serious security and economic unrest.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: The country needed stronger national capacity to maintain order

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which structure existed under the Articles of Confederation?
choices: A one-house Congress with one vote per state
A two-house Congress based only on population
A separately elected national president
A national court system above state courts
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The Articles created a UNICAMERAL legislature. Each state had one vote regardless of population.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: A one-house Congress with one vote per state

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: What did the Articles lack that the Constitution later created?
choices: Separate executive and judicial branches
State legislatures and state courts
A national legislative body
A process for changing the national plan
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The Articles had a Congress but no independent national executive or national judiciary. The Constitution created all three branches.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Separate executive and judicial branches

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Why was changing the Articles nearly impossible?
choices: Every state had to approve an amendment
The president could veto every proposal
The Supreme Court reviewed each change
Voters had to approve changes unanimously
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Amending the Articles required UNANIMOUS approval from all thirteen states.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Every state had to approve an amendment

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which change most directly fixed Congress’s inability to raise money reliably?
choices: The Constitution gave Congress power to levy taxes
The Constitution gave each state one vote
The Constitution required unanimous ratification
The Constitution ended national borrowing
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Article I gives Congress power to lay and collect taxes, providing revenue without depending only on voluntary state payments.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: The Constitution gave Congress power to levy taxes

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which comparison is accurate?
choices: Articles: weak central government; Constitution: stronger national government
Articles: strong president; Constitution: no executive
Articles: national courts; Constitution: state courts only
Articles: federal taxes; Constitution: state requests only
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The biggest shift was from a central government with few independent powers to a stronger national government able to act directly.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Articles: weak central government; Constitution: stronger national government

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: The Articles best reflected which idea about where governing power should remain?
choices: State sovereignty
Judicial supremacy
Executive privilege
National supremacy
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: STATE SOVEREIGNTY was central to the Articles: the states retained most governing power and independence.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: State sovereignty

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Hamilton complains that national laws under the Articles are treated like recommendations. Which constitutional idea addresses that problem?
choices: Valid federal laws are supreme over conflicting state laws
States may ignore federal laws after a referendum
Congress must ask governors before enforcing a law
Federal courts may hear only local disputes
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The SUPREMACY CLAUSE makes valid federal law binding, while the Constitution also lets the national government act directly on individuals.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Valid federal laws are supreme over conflicting state laws

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Large states want representation based on population; small states want equal representation. What settled the dispute?
choices: A House based on population and a Senate with equal state representation
Both chambers based only on population
One chamber with one vote for each state
A president who assigns seats to each state
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The GREAT COMPROMISE created a bicameral Congress: population in the House and equal state representation in the Senate.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: A House based on population and a Senate with equal state representation

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: What was a direct result of the Three-Fifths Compromise?
choices: Enslaved people were partially counted for representation and direct taxes
Three-fifths of enslaved people received voting rights
Amendments required support from three-fifths of the states
Three-fifths of senators came from slave states
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The formula counted every five enslaved people as three for representation and direct taxation, increasing slave states’ political power without granting rights.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Enslaved people were partially counted for representation and direct taxes

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Why did the Electoral College reflect a compromise?
choices: It placed electors between voters and the formal choice of president
It let the Supreme Court select the president
It required Congress to appoint every elector
It gave every state exactly one electoral vote
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Delegates disagreed over direct election and selection by Congress. The ELECTORAL COLLEGE created an indirect process involving the states.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: It placed electors between voters and the formal choice of president

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which constitutional feature most clearly treats the country as a union of states as well as people?
choices: The Electoral College
Judicial review
Cabinet departments
Executive orders
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Electoral votes are assigned through states, combining population-based representation with state-based influence.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: The Electoral College

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: What was the central disagreement between Federalists and Anti-Federalists during ratification?
choices: How powerful the new national government should be
Whether the colonies should declare independence
Whether states should issue any currency
How many justices should sit on the Supreme Court
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The RATIFICATION debate focused on the scope of national power and whether the proposed Constitution adequately protected liberty and the states.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: How powerful the new national government should be

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: What helped win support from people who feared the new Constitution threatened individual liberty?
choices: A promise to add a Bill of Rights
A promise to remove the national legislature
A promise to require unanimous laws
A promise to end state governments
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Federalists promised that the first Congress would propose written protections. That promise helped secure ratification.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: A promise to add a Bill of Rights

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Congress has proposed an amendment. What must happen before it becomes part of the Constitution?
choices: Three-fourths of the states must ratify it
The president must sign it
A national popular majority must approve it
The Supreme Court must rewrite it
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Under ARTICLE V, proposal is only the first stage. Ratification requires approval from three-fourths of the states.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Three-fourths of the states must ratify it

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which is one constitutional way to propose an amendment?
choices: Two-thirds of both houses of Congress approve it
Three-fourths of governors sign it
A majority of voters approve it
The president issues an order
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: An amendment may be proposed by TWO-THIRDS of both houses of Congress or by a convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Two-thirds of both houses of Congress approve it

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Why did the framers make the amendment process difficult?
choices: To allow change while requiring broad and lasting agreement
To prevent the Constitution from ever changing
To let temporary majorities rewrite basic rules quickly
To give the president final control over amendments
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: ARTICLE V balances adaptability with stability. Fundamental change is possible, but it needs broad national and state support.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: To allow change while requiring broad and lasting agreement

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Why is the president’s signature not required for a constitutional amendment?
choices: Article V gives proposal and ratification roles to Congress and the states
The Supreme Court signs amendments instead
Governors replace the president in the process
Amendments become law through executive orders
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The amendment process is separate from ordinary lawmaking. The president has no formal approval role under ARTICLE V.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Article V gives proposal and ratification roles to Congress and the states

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: What principle is shown when both Congress and the states participate in changing the Constitution?
choices: Federalism
Judicial review
Unitary government
Direct democracy
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The process divides responsibility between national and state institutions, illustrating FEDERALISM.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Federalism

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: A popular proposal repeatedly fails to become an amendment. Which explanation is strongest?
choices: Popular support alone does not meet Article V’s supermajority requirements
The president has vetoed it
The Supreme Court refuses to count state votes
Congress cannot propose amendments
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Even a popular idea must pass the Constitution’s demanding proposal and ratification thresholds.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Popular support alone does not meet Article V’s supermajority requirements

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which sequence best explains the founding story?
choices: Fear of tyranny → weak Articles → national problems → stronger but limited Constitution
Strong Articles → state rebellion → weaker Constitution → direct democracy
Bill of Rights → independence → monarchy → national supremacy
Strong presidency → weak states → Articles → unanimous Constitution
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Americans reacted to British power by creating weak national institutions, saw the resulting problems, and then designed stronger but limited national power.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Fear of tyranny → weak Articles → national problems → stronger but limited Constitution

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which example best shows the Constitution solving an Articles-era problem?
choices: Congress regulates trade among states that once used conflicting rules
Each state ignores national policy when it disagrees
A national law requires approval from all fifty states
Congress requests taxes but cannot collect them
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: The Commerce Clause gives Congress authority over interstate commerce, directly addressing a major weakness under the Articles.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Congress regulates trade among states that once used conflicting rules

unit1-history-concept-practice.prompt: Which claim is best supported by both the ratification debate and the Bill of Rights?
choices: Building effective government required answering fears about liberty
The states wanted national power to remain completely unchanged
Federalists and Anti-Federalists agreed on every constitutional power
Written rights made limits on power unnecessary
unit1-history-concept-practice.why: Ratification succeeded partly because supporters answered concerns about stronger power with a promise of explicit protections for liberty.
unit1-history-concept-practice.correct: Building effective government required answering fears about liberty

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: What does separation of powers do?
choices: Gives different government powers to different branches
Gives every branch the same responsibilities
Places all national power in Congress
Lets states control the national branches
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: SEPARATION OF POWERS divides legislative, executive, and judicial authority among three branches.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Gives different government powers to different branches

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Why did the framers divide power among three branches?
choices: To keep power from concentrating in one place
To make every policy decision happen quickly
To eliminate disagreements inside government
To make the executive branch dominant
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Divided power helps prevent TYRANNY and supports LIMITED GOVERNMENT.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: To keep power from concentrating in one place

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: What makes an action a constitutional check rather than just a separate power?
choices: One branch can limit or respond to another branch
A branch performs one of its normal duties
Citizens criticize a public official
Two chambers debate the same bill
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: A CHECK occurs when one branch uses its authority to restrain or respond to another branch.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: One branch can limit or respond to another branch

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: The president vetoes a bill passed by Congress. What does this illustrate?
choices: An executive check on the legislative branch
A judicial check on the executive branch
Federalism between two levels of government
A legislative check on the courts
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: The VETO lets the president block legislation passed by Congress.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: An executive check on the legislative branch

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Congress passes a bill over a presidential veto with the required vote. What does this illustrate?
choices: A legislative check on the executive branch
An executive check on the judicial branch
A state check on the national government
A judicial check on Congress
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: A VETO OVERRIDE allows Congress to check the president with two-thirds support in both chambers.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: A legislative check on the executive branch

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Which action can the Senate use to check a presidential appointment?
choices: Reject the nominee during confirmation
Remove the nominee through a recall election
Declare the nomination unconstitutional
Require the House to choose the nominee
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: The president nominates many officials and federal judges, but the Senate provides ADVICE AND CONSENT.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Reject the nominee during confirmation

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: The president negotiates a treaty. What must happen before it can be ratified?
choices: Two-thirds of the Senate must approve it
A majority of the House must approve it
The Supreme Court must sign it
Three-fourths of the states must approve it
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Treaties negotiated by the president require approval from TWO-THIRDS OF THE SENATE.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Two-thirds of the Senate must approve it

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Which congressional power can restrict a president’s plans by controlling government spending?
choices: Power of the purse
Judicial review
Executive privilege
Senatorial courtesy
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Congress’s POWER OF THE PURSE lets it approve, reduce, or deny money for executive policies.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Power of the purse

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Which process can actually remove a president from office?
choices: The House impeaches and the Senate convicts
Both chambers pass a recall resolution
The Supreme Court conducts an impeachment trial
The Senate impeaches and the House convicts
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: The House brings articles of IMPEACHMENT. The Senate holds the trial and can convict and remove.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: The House impeaches and the Senate convicts

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement about impeachment is accurate?
choices: Impeachment by the House is a charge, not automatic removal
The Senate impeaches before the House investigates
The Supreme Court votes to remove the president
Citizens remove a president through a national recall
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: A House vote to impeach brings charges. Removal requires conviction in a Senate trial.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Impeachment by the House is a charge, not automatic removal

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Congress believes a president has acted unconstitutionally. Which response is a real congressional check?
choices: Use oversight, funding, legislation, or impeachment powers
Pass a law that officially declares the action unconstitutional
Cancel the presidential election results
Order the Supreme Court to remove the president
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Congress has powerful checks, but courts—not Congress—issue controlling judicial rulings about constitutionality.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Use oversight, funding, legislation, or impeachment powers

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: A federal agency issues a rule that violates the Constitution. What can the Supreme Court do?
choices: Declare the rule unconstitutional
Rewrite the rule before it is issued
Remove the agency director through impeachment
Cut the agency’s operating budget
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Through JUDICIAL REVIEW, courts can invalidate unconstitutional executive or legislative actions.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Declare the rule unconstitutional

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: What is a judicial check on Congress?
choices: Strike down a law that violates the Constitution
Review every bill before Congress votes
Remove the Speaker of the House
Refuse to fund a congressional program
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Federal courts can use JUDICIAL REVIEW after a proper case reaches them.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Strike down a law that violates the Constitution

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Which is a legislative check on the judicial branch?
choices: The House impeaches and the Senate may remove a federal judge
Congress overturns a ruling with a simple majority
The House appoints Supreme Court justices
The Senate orders courts to hear particular cases
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Federal judges may be impeached by the House and tried and removed by the Senate.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: The House impeaches and the Senate may remove a federal judge

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: How can Congress affect the structure of the Supreme Court?
choices: Set the number of justices by law
Select the chief justice without the president
Shorten a justice’s term whenever it disagrees
Directly reverse any ruling by resolution
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Congress has authority to establish the size and organization of the federal judiciary, although appointments still involve the president and Senate.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Set the number of justices by law

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: A constitutional amendment is ratified after a Court ruling. How can that affect judicial power?
choices: It can change the constitutional rule the Court must apply
It removes every justice who joined the ruling
It lets Congress ignore the Constitution
It makes the president the final interpreter
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: An AMENDMENT changes the Constitution itself and can therefore alter the rule underlying a judicial decision.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: It can change the constitutional rule the Court must apply

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: A president nominates a Supreme Court justice and the Senate votes on confirmation. Why did the framers divide this job?
choices: Each branch can limit the ambition of the other
The House must control all judicial appointments
Judges should be chosen by direct popular vote
The president should act without outside review
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: The shared appointment power applies Federalist No. 51: ambition in one branch is checked by authority in another.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Each branch can limit the ambition of the other

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Why does the Constitution create tension over military action?
choices: The president commands the military while Congress declares war and funds it
Congress commands troops while courts declare war
States fund all national military operations
The president alone holds every war power
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: War powers are divided: the president is COMMANDER IN CHIEF, while Congress declares war and controls funding.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: The president commands the military while Congress declares war and funds it

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Congress believes the president is using military force too broadly. Which response is a constitutional check?
choices: Limit or deny funding for the operation
Let individual states command federal troops
Ask the president to declare the action illegal
Require the Supreme Court to write a new treaty
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Congress can use legislation and its POWER OF THE PURSE to limit military action.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Limit or deny funding for the operation

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.lesson: FRICTION IS PART OF THE DESIGN
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: The president threatens an executive order because Congress will not pass a climate bill. What does this best illustrate?
choices: Separation of powers can create policy conflict between branches
The branches have identical constitutional powers
The executive branch can permanently replace Congress
Federalism prevents national policy making
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Separate institutions with different powers and goals often disagree, creating deliberate FRICTION in policymaking.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Separation of powers can create policy conflict between branches

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.lesson: FRICTION IS PART OF THE DESIGN
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Why can the lawmaking process be slow even when many people support an idea?
choices: Several institutions must agree before national power is used
The Constitution requires judges to write every bill
Every national law needs approval from the states
The president controls debate in both chambers
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: BICAMERALISM, presidential action, and possible judicial review create multiple decision points.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Several institutions must agree before national power is used

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.lesson: FRICTION IS PART OF THE DESIGN
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: What does bicameralism mean?
choices: Congress has two chambers with different structures and rules
House members serve two-year terms
The president may veto both chambers separately
Congress and the courts share one chamber
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: BICAMERALISM divides Congress into the House of Representatives and the Senate.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Congress has two chambers with different structures and rules

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: What does Madison mean when he says “ambition must be made to counteract ambition”?
choices: Officials should have powers and motives to resist other branches
Candidates should compete for the same office
Congress should control the personal goals of judges
Presidents should appoint ambitious cabinet members
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Each branch needs constitutional tools and institutional motives to defend its authority against encroachment.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Officials should have powers and motives to resist other branches

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: According to Federalist No. 51, why are elections alone not enough to control government?
choices: Government also needs an internal structure that checks power
Voters cannot select any national officials
Elections automatically eliminate factions
Only judges can protect popular government
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Madison calls dependence on the people the primary control, but adds internal checks as an auxiliary precaution.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Government also needs an internal structure that checks power

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Which scenario best reflects Madison’s argument in Federalist No. 51?
choices: The Senate rejects a president’s nominee after reviewing the choice
The president chooses every federal official alone
Congress gives away its lawmaking authority permanently
All three branches agree never to challenge one another
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Senate confirmation gives one branch a constitutional defense against another branch’s appointment power.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: The Senate rejects a president’s nominee after reviewing the choice

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: A law allows the president to launch military strikes anywhere without meaningful congressional involvement. What is the strongest separation-of-powers concern?
choices: Congress may have surrendered a core war power to the executive
The states should negotiate foreign treaties
The judiciary has gained too much budget power
The House is interfering with Senate confirmations
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: The Constitution divides military authority so that one branch cannot control every decision about war.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Congress may have surrendered a core war power to the executive

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: An independent agency writes rules, enforces them, and decides disputes about them. What constitutional concern could this raise?
choices: It combines legislative, executive, and judicial functions
It gives state governments too much authority
It prevents Congress from being bicameral
It makes elections too directly democratic
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Combining several types of power in one body can create a SEPARATION OF POWERS concern.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: It combines legislative, executive, and judicial functions

unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claim that checks and balances protect liberty?
choices: Federalist No. 51 says each branch should resist encroachment by the others
Federalist No. 10 says factions can be eliminated
Brutus No. 1 asks for a stronger executive
Article V lets the president veto amendments
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.why: Federalist No. 51 directly connects divided power and mutual checks to controlling government abuse.
unit1-topic-16-concept-practice.correct: Federalist No. 51 says each branch should resist encroachment by the others

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: What does federalism divide?
choices: Power between the national government and state governments
Power among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches
Authority between voters and political parties
Responsibility between the House and Senate
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: FEDERALISM divides governing authority between the national government and state governments.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Power between the national government and state governments

choices: The enumerated power to regulate interstate commerce

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Congress creates a federal agency to help carry out one of its listed powers. What kind of power is it using?

A reserved power protected from federal use
An exclusive power belonging to the states
A judicial power created by precedent
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: IMPLIED POWERS are reasonable means used to carry out Congress’s enumerated powers.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: An implied power connected to an enumerated power

choices: The Necessary and Proper Clause
The Full Faith and Credit Clause

The Establishment Clause

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: The Necessary and Proper Clause

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: A state sets licensing requirements for nurses working inside the state. Which category best fits this authority?
choices: Reserved power
Enumerated power
Implied power
Exclusive national power
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Professional licensing is a common RESERVED POWER retained by the states under the Tenth Amendment.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Reserved power

choices: Powers not delegated to the United States or prohibited to the states
Every power that Congress has not used recently
Only the powers specifically listed in the amendment
The authority to cancel any federal law
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: The TENTH AMENDMENT reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Powers not delegated to the United States or prohibited to the states

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Residents pay both state and federal income taxes. What does this illustrate?
choices: Concurrent powers
Reserved powers
Exclusive powers
Judicial powers
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: CONCURRENT POWERS may be exercised by both national and state governments. Taxation is a major example.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Concurrent powers

States may automatically override national laws

Courts prevent the two levels from sharing responsibilities
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Because both levels can act in the same area, they often share funding, administration, or enforcement.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Both levels may act in the same policy area

choices: The valid federal law takes precedence
The state law always takes precedence
Both laws become unenforceable
The governor chooses which law controls

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: The valid federal law takes precedence

Congress needs permission from every governor
The Supreme Court writes all federal statutes

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Federal law is supreme only when Congress is using a constitutional power

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Why does Madison call the Constitution “a composition of both” federal and national features?
choices: Some features preserve states as units while others act on or represent the people nationally
The Constitution divides power equally among all governments
Every national official is selected by state legislatures
The states and Congress must approve every federal law
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: FEDERALIST NO. 39 explains that the system mixes state-based features with features that operate on the nation and its people.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Some features preserve states as units while others act on or represent the people nationally

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Why can public education policy look different from one state to another?
choices: Federalism allows states to make many of their own policy choices
Separation of powers gives schools control over Congress
The Supremacy Clause prevents national education funding
Judicial review requires every state to experiment

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Federalism allows states to make many of their own policy choices

The president created the bank through an executive order

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: The bank was a reasonable means of carrying out enumerated fiscal powers

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Why could Maryland not tax the national bank?
choices: A state could not interfere with a valid federal institution
The Constitution prohibits every state tax
Only federal courts may collect taxes
Banks are protected by the First Amendment
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: The SUPREMACY CLAUSE prevented Maryland from taxing and interfering with a constitutional federal instrument.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: A state could not interfere with a valid federal institution

It ended Congress’s ability to regulate the economy
It made state governments superior to Congress

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: It strengthened national power through implied powers and federal supremacy

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: What federal law was challenged in United States v. Lopez?
choices: A law banning gun possession in a school zone
A law creating a national bank

A law funding interstate highways
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: LOPEZ involved the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: A law banning gun possession in a school zone

choices: Gun possession near a school was too weakly connected to interstate commerce
Education is listed as an exclusive national power
The law violated the Supremacy Clause
Congress may regulate only foreign commerce
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: The Court held that Congress had exceeded its COMMERCE CLAUSE authority.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Gun possession near a school was too weakly connected to interstate commerce

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: What did the Lopez decision recognize about national power?
choices: Congress’s commerce power has constitutional limits
States may ignore all federal gun laws
Congress cannot regulate any economic activity
Schools are controlled by federal courts
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: LOPEZ marked a limit on the use of the Commerce Clause and protected an area of state authority.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Congress’s commerce power has constitutional limits

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Which comparison between McCulloch and Lopez is accurate?

McCulloch limited commerce power; Lopez created implied powers
Both cases made state law supreme over federal law
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Together the cases show that federal power is substantial but not unlimited.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: McCulloch affirmed national power; Lopez enforced a limit on national power

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Which constitutional provision has often been used to expand national regulation of the economy?
choices: The Commerce Clause
The Tenth Amendment
The Ex Post Facto Clause
The Guarantee Clause
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Broad interpretations of the COMMERCE CLAUSE have supported extensive national regulation of interstate economic activity.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: The Commerce Clause

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: A Court decision permits Congress to regulate factory labor because it substantially affects interstate commerce. What happens to the federal balance?
choices: National regulatory power expands
Reserved powers disappear completely

Congress loses its implied powers
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: A broad connection to interstate commerce increases the range of activity Congress may regulate.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: National regulatory power expands

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: A state immigration rule conflicts with a valid federal immigration rule. What is the strongest constitutional basis for setting aside the state rule?
choices: The Supremacy Clause
The Tenth Amendment
The Establishment Clause
The Contracts Clause
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Federal law may PREEMPT conflicting state law when the national government is acting constitutionally.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: The Supremacy Clause

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: American federalism combines separate, shared, and overlapping powers rather than creating a perfectly strict division.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: National and state governments have separate and overlapping powers, with valid federal law controlling conflicts

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: A state creates its own health-care program even though the national government has not adopted that policy. What does this show?

Federal courts control state budgets
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: States remain meaningful policy-making governments and may act where federal law does not prevent them.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: States can use reserved authority to pursue policies independently

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Which form of federal aid usually gives states the broadest discretion?
choices: Block grants
Categorical grants
Unfunded mandates
Project requirements

choices: Categorical grant
Block grant
Revenue sharing without conditions
Reserved power
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: CATEGORICAL GRANTS fund a specific purpose and come with more detailed federal requirements.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Categorical grant

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: The state has more freedom to decide how the money is used

A block grant
A reserved power
Revenue sharing
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: An UNFUNDED MANDATE requires action without providing the funds needed to carry it out.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: An unfunded mandate

choices: A federal mandate
A concurrent tax
A block grant
A state compact
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: A FEDERAL MANDATE directs state or local governments to meet a national requirement.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: A federal mandate

choices: Attaching conditions to federal funds

Giving states an unfunded mandate

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Congress can use its TAXING AND SPENDING POWER to encourage state action by placing conditions on federal grants.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Attaching conditions to federal funds

choices: Federal influence through conditional aid
Exclusive state control over education
Horizontal federalism among states
Judicial review of school policy

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Federal influence through conditional aid

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: The national government replaces a detailed federal welfare program with broad grants administered by states. What trend does this reflect?
choices: Devolution of responsibility to the states
Nationalization of local elections
Expansion of judicial review
Elimination of fiscal federalism
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: DEVOLUTION shifts administrative responsibility and discretion from the national government toward the states.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Devolution of responsibility to the states

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: What does fiscal federalism describe?
choices: How federal money and conditions shape relations with states
How courts divide cases between jurisdictions
How states recognize one another’s laws
How Congress divides taxes between its chambers
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: FISCAL FEDERALISM concerns grants, funding conditions, and other financial relationships between levels of government.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: How federal money and conditions shape relations with states

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: A map shows large differences among states in health-insurance coverage. Which principle best helps explain the variation?
choices: Federalism
Bicameralism
Judicial restraint
Separation of powers
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: States make different policy choices and administer shared programs differently, producing POLICY VARIATION.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Federalism

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Why does federalism give interest groups multiple access points?
choices: Groups may seek change from national, state, or local officials
Every policy must be approved by all fifty states
State courts write federal legislation
Congress controls every local agency
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Power is spread across levels of government, so citizens and groups can pursue policy change in more than one place.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: Groups may seek change from national, state, or local officials

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: One state tests a new election system while other states keep their current rules. Which consequence of federalism does this show?
choices: States can serve as policy laboratories
Federal law must be identical in every state
Concurrent powers eliminate experimentation
National supremacy prevents local innovation
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Federalism allows states to experiment with different policies and lets others evaluate the results.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: States can serve as policy laboratories

unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement best captures federalism in action?
choices: National and state governments share, compete for, and negotiate power through laws, courts, and money
The Constitution permanently separates every policy area
State governments administer policy without national influence
The national government depends on states for every valid action
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.why: Federalism is an ongoing relationship shaped by constitutional powers, court interpretations, grants, and mandates.
unit1-topic-17-19-concept-practice.correct: National and state governments share, compete for, and negotiate power through laws, courts, and money

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A senator uses extended debate to delay a bill until its supporters agree to changes. Which Senate procedure is being used?
choices: A discharge petition
A filibuster
A conference committee
A veto
unit2-concept-practice.why: A filibuster uses extended Senate debate to delay or block action. The House limits debate more tightly through its formal rules.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: A filibuster

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A senator wants to end debate and move the chamber toward a vote. Which procedure should the senator support?
choices: Cloture
Reapportionment
A line-item veto
A discharge petition
unit2-concept-practice.why: Cloture is the Senate procedure for ending debate, often to overcome a filibuster.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Cloture

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which feature best describes a standing committee in Congress?
choices: A temporary group formed only to reconcile two bill versions
A permanent committee focused on a policy area
A committee made up of members from both chambers that elects the president
A group of advisers appointed by the president
unit2-concept-practice.why: Standing committees are continuing, subject-matter committees. They review bills and build expertise in policy areas.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: A permanent committee focused on a policy area

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: The House and Senate pass different versions of the same bill. What is the usual next step to resolve the differences?
choices: A conference committee works out a compromise
The Supreme Court selects one version
The president rewrites the bill
The House Rules Committee votes for both chambers
unit2-concept-practice.why: A conference committee, with members from both chambers, negotiates a version that can return to the House and Senate for approval.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: A conference committee works out a compromise

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which House committee most directly determines the terms for floor debate and which amendments may be considered on many bills?
choices: Ways and Means
Rules
Agriculture
Appropriations
unit2-concept-practice.why: The House Rules Committee sets debate conditions, including time limits and amendment rules, giving it substantial influence over the floor process.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Rules

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: The Speaker’s floor team is coordinating the majority party’s schedule and building support for upcoming House votes. Which leader most directly manages that floor work?
choices: The House majority leader
The Senate president pro tempore
The vice president
The House minority whip
unit2-concept-practice.why: The House majority leader helps shape the majority party’s legislative agenda and coordinates floor work with the Speaker.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: The House majority leader

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: What is a central role of a party whip in either chamber?
choices: Preside over federal impeachment trials
Track votes and build support for party positions
Judge whether new federal laws are constitutional
Choose committee chairs for the opposite chamber
unit2-concept-practice.why: Whips track likely votes and communicate with members to build support for party priorities.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Track votes and build support for party positions

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Why do committees help Congress process legislation?
choices: They replace elections as the source of congressional authority
They let members develop expertise and examine bills in detail
They prevent the public from learning about proposed laws
They guarantee that every bill reaches the floor
unit2-concept-practice.why: The committee system divides a large workload and lets members develop policy expertise. Committees can also hold hearings, revise bills, or decline to advance them.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: They let members develop expertise and examine bills in detail

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A committee investigates whether a federal agency is carrying out a law as Congress intended. This is an example of Congress using its
choices: oversight function
treaty power
judicial review
executive privilege
unit2-concept-practice.why: Congress uses oversight to monitor how the executive branch and federal agencies implement laws.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: oversight function

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which statement best describes how seniority can affect committee leadership?
choices: The Constitution gives every long-serving member a chair
Seniority can influence, but not decide, chair selection
The president selects committee chairs
The minority party chairs the largest committees
unit2-concept-practice.why: Seniority has often influenced committee leadership, especially among majority-party members, but the Constitution does not require the most senior member to become chair.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Seniority can influence, but not decide, chair selection

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which member is generally eligible to chair a House committee under the chamber’s party organization?
choices: A member of the majority party selected under House rules
A senator appointed by the president
The most senior member of the minority party by constitutional requirement
The House minority whip automatically
unit2-concept-practice.why: House committee chairs are selected from the majority party under the chamber’s organizational rules. Seniority may matter, but it does not automatically determine the chair.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: A member of the majority party selected under House rules

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Congress creates a national agency to set workplace safety standards, linking the law to its authority over interstate commerce. Which constitutional idea supports this action?
choices: Congress’s implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause
The Senate’s power to approve treaties with foreign governments
The House’s power to impeach federal officers
The president’s power to pardon federal offenders
unit2-concept-practice.why: Congress may use implied powers—authority reasonably connected to enumerated powers—to carry out its constitutional responsibilities. The Necessary and Proper Clause supports laws that implement enumerated powers.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Congress’s implied powers under the Necessary and Proper Clause

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which comparison of representation in the House and Senate is accurate?
choices: Both chambers give every state equal representation
House seats follow population; every state has two senators
Senate seats follow population; House seats are equal
House seats follow land area; Senate seats follow population
unit2-concept-practice.why: House seats are apportioned among states by population. The Senate gives each state equal representation with two senators.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: House seats follow population; every state has two senators

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Why is a House member’s constituency generally smaller than a senator’s constituency?
choices: House members represent a state’s entire population
House members represent districts; senators represent entire states
House members are appointed by local governments and may change
Senators represent only major cities within their states
unit2-concept-practice.why: Each representative serves a congressional district. Each senator represents the whole state.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: House members represent districts; senators represent entire states

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A bill to raise federal revenue is introduced in Congress. Where must it begin under the Constitution?
choices: The Senate
The House of Representatives
A conference committee
The president’s Cabinet
unit2-concept-practice.why: The Constitution requires bills for raising revenue to originate in the House, though the Senate may propose or concur with amendments.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: The House of Representatives

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which power belongs specifically to the Senate?
choices: Starting federal revenue bills
Confirming nominees such as ambassadors
Approving articles of impeachment
Setting debate rules for the House
unit2-concept-practice.why: The Senate confirms ambassadors and other presidential nominees. The House starts revenue bills and approves articles of impeachment.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Confirming nominees such as ambassadors

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: The House votes to impeach a federal official. Which chamber conducts the trial?
choices: The Senate
The Supreme Court
The House Rules Committee
The Cabinet
unit2-concept-practice.why: The House has the sole power to impeach; the Senate has the sole power to try impeachments.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: The Senate

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which chamber is more likely to rely on formal limits on debate because it has many more members?
choices: The House, because its membership is much larger
The Senate, because members represent whole states
Both chambers use identical debate rules
Neither chamber may set debate rules
unit2-concept-practice.why: The House’s larger membership makes structured debate rules important. Senate debate is generally less restricted, which gives individual senators more opportunity to delay action.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: The House, because its membership is much larger

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A senator argues that a bill should be delayed unless its supporters address the minority’s concerns. Which institutional feature gives the senator more leverage than a House member?
choices: The Senate’s tradition of extended debate
The Senate’s power to originate revenue bills
The House’s larger constituencies
The Senate’s power to appoint committee chairs in the House
unit2-concept-practice.why: The Senate’s extended-debate tradition allows a determined minority to delay action. Cloture can be used to end debate.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: The Senate’s tradition of extended debate

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches a chamber with one of its constitutional responsibilities?
choices: House — confirms presidential appointments
Senate — tries impeachments
House — ratifies treaties
Senate — originates revenue bills
unit2-concept-practice.why: The Senate tries impeachments. The Senate also confirms nominees and consents to treaties; revenue bills begin in the House.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Senate — tries impeachments

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A legislator wants to bring a bill out of committee despite opposition from its chair. Which House procedure may help force a bill to the floor?
choices: A discharge petition
Cloture
A pocket veto
A conference report
unit2-concept-practice.why: A discharge petition can bring a measure out of committee when enough House members sign it, bypassing the committee chair’s control.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: A discharge petition

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A representative secures federal funding for a local bridge project and highlights it to district voters. Which concept best describes this strategy?
choices: Pork-barrel politics
Judicial review
Cloture
Executive agreement
unit2-concept-practice.why: Pork-barrel politics directs government spending toward projects intended to benefit a member’s district or state, often helping the member demonstrate service to constituents.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Pork-barrel politics

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A representative agrees to support a colleague’s transportation bill after the colleague promises to support a farm bill. Which practice does this illustrate?
choices: Logrolling
Oversight
Cloture
Reapportionment
unit2-concept-practice.why: Logrolling is an exchange of legislative support: members agree to back one another’s proposals, often to build coalitions for measures important to their constituencies.
unit2-concept-practice.correct: Logrolling

unit2-concept-practice.prompt: A bill would create federal workplace safety standards. Members of which congressional body are most likely to examine the bill’s details and hear from specialists before it reaches the floor?
choices: A relevant standing committee or subcommittee
The Electoral College
The Cabinet
A federal court of appeals
unit2-concept-practice.why: Standing committees and their subcommittees handle policy areas over time. Hearings and detailed review let members gather information and revise proposals.
